claim: Changes in DNA methylation are involved in development.
source: Changes in DNA methylation are involved in development, disease, and the response to environmental conditions.
evidence: Supported by citation to Smith and Meissner, 2013

claim: Changes in DNA methylation are involved in disease.
source: Changes in DNA methylation are involved in development, disease, and the response to environmental conditions.
evidence: Supported by citations to El-Maarri, 2005 and Heyn and Esteller, 2012

claim: Changes in DNA methylation are involved in the response to environmental conditions.
source: Changes in DNA methylation are involved in development, disease, and the response to environmental conditions.
evidence: Supported by citations to Jirtle and Skinner, 2007; Feil and Fraga, 2012; Joshi et al., 2018

claim: Not all regulatory elements are functionally methylation-dependent (MD).
source: However, not all regulatory elements are functionally methylation-dependent (MD).
evidence: This is a key premise of the study, supported by subsequent experimental data showing heterogeneity in MD activity

claim: mSTARR-seq assesses the causal effects of DNA methylation on regulatory activity at hundreds of thousands of fragments simultaneously.
source: Here, we report a method, mSTARR-seq, that assesses the causal effects of DNA methylation on regulatory activity at hundreds of thousands of fragments (millions of CpG sites) simultaneously.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing ~750,000 unique DNA fragments were assayed

claim: mSTARR-seq identifies thousands of MD regulatory elements in the human genome.
source: Using mSTARR-seq, we identify thousands of MD regulatory elements in the human genome.
evidence: Supported by experimental data identifying 2969 MD enhancers

claim: MD activity is partially predictable using sequence and chromatin state information.
source: MD activity is partially predictable using sequence and chromatin state information, and distinct transcription factors are associated with higher activity in unmethylated versus methylated DNA.
evidence: Supported by random forests analysis showing 78.8% prediction accuracy

claim: Distinct transcription factors are associated with higher activity in unmethylated versus methylated DNA.
source: MD activity is partially predictable using sequence and chromatin state information, and distinct transcription factors are associated with higher activity in unmethylated versus methylated DNA.
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analyses showing different TF families enriched in MD enhancers with different activity patterns

claim: Pioneer TFs linked to higher activity in the methylated state appear to drive demethylation of experimentally methylated sites.
source: Further, pioneer TFs linked to higher activity in the methylated state appear to drive demethylation of experimentally methylated sites.
evidence: Supported by bisulfite sequencing data showing demethylation at GATA family TF binding sites

claim: MD regulatory elements predict methylation-gene expression relationships across individuals.
source: MD regulatory elements also predict methylation-gene expression relationships across individuals, where they are 1.6x enriched among sites with strong negative correlations.
evidence: Supported by analysis of 1202 human monocyte samples showing enrichment of significant correlations in MD enhancers

claim: MD regulatory elements are 1.6x enriched among sites with strong negative correlations between methylation and gene expression.
source: MD regulatory elements also predict methylation-gene expression relationships across individuals, where they are 1.6x enriched among sites with strong negative correlations.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of monocyte data

claim: Epigenome-wide association studies (EWAS) have identified thousands of correlations between DNA methylation levels at individual CpG sites and age.
source: In support of this argument, epigenome-wide association studies (EWAS) have identified thousands of correlations between DNA methylation levels at individual CpG sites and age (Winnefeld and Lyko, 2012; Day et al., 2013; Marioni et al., 2015), short-term (Barrès et al., 2012; Pacis et al., 2015) and long-term (Dominguez-Salas et al., 2014; Tobi et al., 2014) reactions to environmental perturbations, and disease, including cancer (Hansen et al., 2011; Hinoue et al., 2012; Aran et al., 2013), type II diabetes (Dayeh et al., 2014), and Alzheimer's disease (Bakulskia et al., 2012; De Jager et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple EWAS studies

claim: EWAS have identified thousands of correlations between DNA methylation levels and short-term reactions to environmental perturbations.
source: In support of this argument, epigenome-wide association studies (EWAS) have identified thousands of correlations between DNA methylation levels at individual CpG sites and age (Winnefeld and Lyko, 2012; Day et al., 2013; Marioni et al., 2015), short-term (Barrès et al., 2012; Pacis et al., 2015) and long-term (Dominguez-Salas et al., 2014; Tobi et al., 2014) reactions to environmental perturbations, and disease, including cancer (Hansen et al., 2011; Hinoue et al., 2012; Aran et al., 2013), type II diabetes (Dayeh et al., 2014), and Alzheimer's disease (Bakulskia et al., 2012; De Jager et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barrès et al., 2012 and Pacis et al., 2015

claim: EWAS have identified thousands of correlations between DNA methylation levels and long-term reactions to environmental perturbations.
source: In support of this argument, epigenome-wide association studies (EWAS) have identified thousands of correlations between DNA methylation levels at individual CpG sites and age (Winnefeld and Lyko, 2012; Day et al., 2013; Marioni et al., 2015), short-term (Barrès et al., 2012; Pacis et al., 2015) and long-term (Dominguez-Salas et al., 2014; Tobi et al., 2014) reactions to environmental perturbations, and disease, including cancer (Hansen et al., 2011; Hinoue et al., 2012; Aran et al., 2013), type II diabetes (Dayeh et al., 2014), and Alzheimer's disease (Bakulskia et al., 2012; De Jager et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dominguez-Salas et al., 2014 and Tobi et al., 2014

claim: EWAS have identified thousands of correlations between DNA methylation levels and cancer.
source: In support of this argument, epigenome-wide association studies (EWAS) have identified thousands of correlations between DNA methylation levels at individual CpG sites and age (Winnefeld and Lyko, 2012; Day et al., 2013; Marioni et al., 2015), short-term (Barrès et al., 2012; Pacis et al., 2015) and long-term (Dominguez-Salas et al., 2014; Tobi et al., 2014) reactions to environmental perturbations, and disease, including cancer (Hansen et al., 2011; Hinoue et al., 2012; Aran et al., 2013), type II diabetes (Dayeh et al., 2014), and Alzheimer's disease (Bakulskia et al., 2012; De Jager et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hansen et al., 2011; Hinoue et al., 2012; Aran et al., 2013

claim: EWAS have identified thousands of correlations between DNA methylation levels and type II diabetes.
source: In support of this argument, epigenome-wide association studies (EWAS) have identified thousands of correlations between DNA methylation levels at individual CpG sites and age (Winnefeld and Lyko, 2012; Day et al., 2013; Marioni et al., 2015), short-term (Barrès et al., 2012; Pacis et al., 2015) and long-term (Dominguez-Salas et al., 2014; Tobi et al., 2014) reactions to environmental perturbations, and disease, including cancer (Hansen et al., 2011; Hinoue et al., 2012; Aran et al., 2013), type II diabetes (Dayeh et al., 2014), and Alzheimer's disease (Bakulskia et al., 2012; De Jager et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dayeh et al., 2014

claim: EWAS have identified thousands of correlations between DNA methylation levels and Alzheimer's disease.
source: In support of this argument, epigenome-wide association studies (EWAS) have identified thousands of correlations between DNA methylation levels at individual CpG sites and age (Winnefeld and Lyko, 2012; Day et al., 2013; Marioni et al., 2015), short-term (Barrès et al., 2012; Pacis et al., 2015) and long-term (Dominguez-Salas et al., 2014; Tobi et al., 2014) reactions to environmental perturbations, and disease, including cancer (Hansen et al., 2011; Hinoue et al., 2012; Aran et al., 2013), type II diabetes (Dayeh et al., 2014), and Alzheimer's disease (Bakulskia et al., 2012; De Jager et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bakulskia et al., 2012 and De Jager et al., 2014

claim: Targeted demethylation of CpG sites within the human HBB promoter using TALE-TET1 fusion proteins revealed that demethylation of some CpG sites causally alters gene transcription.
source: For example, targeted demethylation of CpG sites within the human HBB promoter using TALE-TET1 fusion proteins revealed that demethylation of some CpG sites causally alters gene transcription (Maeder et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maeder et al., 2013

claim: Demethylation of some CpG sites in the HBB promoter had no effect on HBB expression.
source: At other CpG sites in the same promoter, however, demethylation had no effect on HBB expression.
evidence: Inferred from the work of Maeder et al., 2013

claim: Current approaches for assaying MD activity either do not provide locus-specific information or can only assay a single locus per experiment.
source: However, current approaches for assaying MD activity are limited, as they either do not provide locus-specific information (Christman, 2002) or can only assay a single locus per experiment (Rivenbark et al., 2012; Maeder et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2016) (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by citations and Table 1 showing limitations of existing methods

claim: Large-scale analyses of MD activity to date have been restricted to in vitro assays performed on sheared or synthesized DNA.
source: Large-scale analyses to date have thus been restricted to in vitro assays performed on sheared or synthesized DNA (Hu et al., 2013; Mann et al., 2013; O'Malley et al., 2016; Zuo et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple in vitro studies

claim: In vitro studies suggest widespread differential TF sensitivity to DNA methylation levels.
source: These studies suggest widespread differential TF sensitivity to DNA methylation levels (Hu et al., 2013; O'Malley et al., 2016; Yin et al., 2017; Zuo et al., 2017), but leave open whether and to what degree differential sensitivity translates to differences in gene expression itself.
evidence: Supported by citations to in vitro TF binding studies

claim: The pmSTARRseq1 vector is CpG-free.
source: To eliminate these confounds, we therefore engineered a novel CpG-free vector (pmSTARRseq1) that eliminates the possibility of bacterial Dam or Dcm-mediated methylation (Figure 1A; Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by the experimental design and vector construction described in Materials and methods

claim: The pmSTARRseq1 vector eliminates the possibility of bacterial Dam or Dcm-mediated methylation.
source: To eliminate these confounds, we therefore engineered a novel CpG-free vector (pmSTARRseq1) that eliminates the possibility of bacterial Dam or Dcm-mediated methylation (Figure 1A; Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by the vector design lacking Dam and Dcm methylation targets

claim: mSTARR-seq assayed ~750,000 unique DNA fragments.
source: Using mSTARR-seq, we assayed ~750,000 unique DNA fragments (mean ± SD = 759,725±252,187 fragments per replicate; Figure 1D), comparable to or exceeding the diversity in published STARR-seq and massively parallel reporter assay experiments (Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental sequencing data

claim: The mSTARR-seq data set covered 1.81 million unique CpG sites.
source: The resulting data set covered 1.81 million unique CpG sites, 57% of fragments expected from a complete MspI digest of the human genome, and 13% of the K562 euchromatic genome (Figure 2A), (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data analysis

claim: The mSTARR-seq data set covered 57% of fragments expected from a complete MspI digest of the human genome.
source: The resulting data set covered 1.81 million unique CpG sites, 57% of fragments expected from a complete MspI digest of the human genome, and 13% of the K562 euchromatic genome (Figure 2A), (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by comparison to in silico MspI digest

claim: The mSTARR-seq data set covered 13% of the K562 euchromatic genome.
source: The resulting data set covered 1.81 million unique CpG sites, 57% of fragments expected from a complete MspI digest of the human genome, and 13% of the K562 euchromatic genome (Figure 2A), (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by genomic coverage analysis

claim: 19,703 intervals showed regulatory/enhancer activity in at least one condition.
source: Within this data set, we identified 19,703 intervals with an excess of plasmid-derived mRNA relative to DNA input in at least one condition (unmethylated or methylated), which indicates regulatory/enhancer activity (8% of analyzed regions; linear model, FDR < 10%: Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by linear model analysis of mRNA/DNA ratios

claim: 2969 regions exhibited significant methylation-dependent (MD) activity.
source: Among regions with evidence for enhancer activity, 2969 exhibited significant methylation-dependent (MD) activity (15% of analyzed regions; linear model, FDR < 10%).
evidence: Supported by linear model analysis with interaction term

claim: 86% of MD enhancers were more active when unmethylated.
source: Eighty-six percent of these MD enhancers were more active when unmethylated and 14% were more active when methylated (Figure 3A; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of MD enhancer activity patterns

claim: 14% of MD enhancers were more active when methylated.
source: Eighty-six percent of these MD enhancers were more active when unmethylated and 14% were more active when methylated (Figure 3A; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of MD enhancer activity patterns

claim: Only 4 of the 325 CpG-free regions in the analysis set were inferred to have MD activity.
source: Only 4 of the 325 CpG-free regions in the analysis set were inferred to have MD activity, consistent with an overall low false discovery rate (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by analysis of CpG-free regions as negative controls

claim: Regions with significant regulatory activity are enriched for enhancer chromatin states in K562 cells.
source: Regions with significant regulatory activity are enriched for enhancer chromatin states in K562 cells (blue). Y-axis shows the two-sided Fisher's Exact Test log2(odds) for enrichment/depletion of mSTARR-seq enhancers in 15 K562-annotated chromatin states (p<0.05 for all tests except 'Weak promoter').
evidence: Supported by Fisher's exact test comparing mSTARR-seq enhancers to ENCODE chromatin states, shown in Figure 2A

claim: mSTARR-seq enhancer activity explains 86.0% of variance in normalized luciferase activity for enhancer detection.
source: mSTARR-seq activity explains 86.0% and 76.1% (p < 10−15) of variance in normalized luciferase activity, respectively (linear mixed model controlling for batch and assay fragment length).
evidence: Supported by validation experiments comparing mSTARR-seq to luciferase assays, shown in Figure 2C

claim: mSTARR-seq MD activity explains 76.1% of variance in normalized luciferase activity for MD-dependent activity.
source: mSTARR-seq activity explains 86.0% and 76.1% (p < 10−15) of variance in normalized luciferase activity, respectively (linear mixed model controlling for batch and assay fragment length).
evidence: Supported by validation experiments comparing mSTARR-seq to luciferase assays, shown in Figure 2C

claim: MD enhancers have higher CpG densities than non-MD enhancers.
source: Overall, we found that MD enhancers have higher CpG densities and contain more CpG sites than non-MD enhancers (two-sided Wilcoxon-signed rank test, p < 10−15; Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of CpG density distributions, shown in Figure 3C

claim: MD enhancers contain more CpG sites than non-MD enhancers.
source: Overall, we found that MD enhancers have higher CpG densities and contain more CpG sites than non-MD enhancers (two-sided Wilcoxon-signed rank test, p < 10−15; Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of CpG number distributions, shown in Figure 3C

claim: CpG density explains only a small amount of variation in the magnitude of methylation dependence (Spearman's rho = 0.284).
source: However, CpG density explained only a small amount of variation in the magnitude of methylation dependence, suggesting that other characteristics also contribute to quantitative variation in MD activity (Spearman's rho = 0.284, p < 10−15; Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3D

claim: The random forests model predicted MD regulatory element activity with 78.8% accuracy.
source: The resulting RF model predicted MD regulatory element activity with 78.8% accuracy (72.3% without the top features of CpG density and CpG number; Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by random forests classification results shown in Figure 3E

claim: 26 features were identified as significant predictors of MD activity.
source: In addition to CpG number and density, 26 features were identified as significant predictors (permutation-based (Archer, 2015) FDR < 10%; Figure 3F and Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Supported by random forests feature importance analysis shown in Figure 3F

claim: MD enhancers suppressed by DNA methylation were more likely to occur in open chromatin than non-MD enhancers.
source: Measures of DNase I hypersensitivity and endogenous methylation levels were among the top predictive features: relative to non-MD enhancers, enhancers suppressed by DNA methylation were more likely to occur in open chromatin or in highly methylated regions of the genome.
evidence: Supported by random forests feature importance analysis

claim: MD enhancers suppressed by DNA methylation were more likely to occur in highly methylated regions of the genome than non-MD enhancers.
source: Measures of DNase I hypersensitivity and endogenous methylation levels were among the top predictive features: relative to non-MD enhancers, enhancers suppressed by DNA methylation were more likely to occur in open chromatin or in highly methylated regions of the genome.
evidence: Supported by random forests feature importance analysis

claim: MD enhancers were more likely to contain binding sites for TFs that contain CpG sites in their canonical binding motifs.
source: MD enhancers were also more likely to contain binding sites for TFs that contain CpG sites in their canonical binding motifs (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by TF binding site analysis shown in Figure 3F

claim: 32 TF-binding motifs were significantly enriched in MD enhancers where DNA methylation suppresses activity.
source: Among the 2543 MD enhancers in which DNA methylation suppresses activity, we identified 32 significantly enriched TF-binding motifs (relative to all regions with mSTARR-seq regulatory activity, FDR < 1%; Figure 4A and Supplementary file 7).
evidence: Supported by HOMER motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4A

claim: Motif enrichment from mSTARR-seq-identified MD enhancers is significantly correlated with estimates of affinity for methylated DNA in SELEX experiments for TFs that preferentially bound unmethylated DNA (R2 = 0.342; p = 1.33 × 10−6).
source: Specifically, when we compared estimates of motif enrichment from mSTARR-seq-identified MD enhancers versus estimates of affinity for methylated DNA in SELEX experiments, we found significant agreement for both TFs that preferentially bound unmethylated (linear model, R2 = 0.342; p = 1.33 × 10−6) and TFs that preferentially bound methylated DNA (linear model, R2 = 0.113, p = 0.028; Figure 5A–B).
evidence: Supported by comparison to Yin et al. 2017 SELEX data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Motif enrichment from mSTARR-seq-identified MD enhancers is significantly correlated with estimates of affinity for methylated DNA in SELEX experiments for TFs that preferentially bound methylated DNA (R2 = 0.113, p = 0.028).
source: Specifically, when we compared estimates of motif enrichment from mSTARR-seq-identified MD enhancers versus estimates of affinity for methylated DNA in SELEX experiments, we found significant agreement for both TFs that preferentially bound unmethylated (linear model, R2 = 0.342; p = 1.33 × 10−6) and TFs that preferentially bound methylated DNA (linear model, R2 = 0.113, p = 0.028; Figure 5A–B).
evidence: Supported by comparison to Yin et al. 2017 SELEX data shown in Figure 5B

claim: 13 TF motifs were associated with increased enhancer activity when DNA was methylated.
source: Among the 13 TF motifs associated with increased enhancer activity when DNA was methylated, we identified a strong overrepresentation of TFs from the GATA subfamily of zinc finger TFs (15.9x enrichment, hypergeometric test p=1.74×10−8; Figure 4B and Supplementary file 8).
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: GATA subfamily TFs are overrepresented among TF motifs associated with increased enhancer activity when DNA was methylated (15.9x enrichment, p=1.74×10−8).
source: Among the 13 TF motifs associated with increased enhancer activity when DNA was methylated, we identified a strong overrepresentation of TFs from the GATA subfamily of zinc finger TFs (15.9x enrichment, hypergeometric test p=1.74×10−8; Figure 4B and Supplementary file 8).
evidence: Supported by hypergeometric test of TF family enrichment

claim: GATA3 and GATA4 can bind to methylated DNA outside the cellular context.
source: This observation is consistent with reports that GATA3 and GATA4 can bind to methylated DNA outside the cellular context (Hu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hu et al., 2013

claim: For five of ten tested GATA family TFs, open chromatin regions specific to wild type murine stem cells were significantly enriched for their cognate-binding sites.
source: For five of ten tested GATA family TFs, open chromatin regions specific to wild type (i.e. those absent in the triple knockouts) were significantly enriched for their cognate-binding sites (Figure 4C), in support of the idea that GATA family TFs preferentially bind methylated DNA as part of their 'pioneer' factor activity (Zhu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by analysis of DNMT knockout data shown in Figure 4C

claim: ETS family TF binding sites were enriched in DNMT knockout-specific open chromatin regions (38 of 41 tested).
source: In contrast, ETS family TF binding sites were almost universally (38 of 41 tested) enriched in DNMT knockout-specific open chromatin regions.
evidence: Supported by analysis of DNMT knockout data shown in Figure 4C

claim: CpG sites in fragments that mapped to the human genome partially converged towards endogenous levels in K562s for unmethylated replicates (rho = 0.476, p<10−16).
source: However, CpG sites in fragments that mapped to the human genome partially converged towards endogenous levels in K562s, for both unmethylated (rho = 0.476, p<10−16) and methylated replicates (rho = 0.223, p<10−16; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: CpG sites in fragments that mapped to the human genome partially converged towards endogenous levels in K562s for methylated replicates (rho = 0.223, p<10−16).
source: However, CpG sites in fragments that mapped to the human genome partially converged towards endogenous levels in K562s, for both unmethylated (rho = 0.476, p<10−16) and methylated replicates (rho = 0.223, p<10−16; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: 23.1% of sites in the unmethylated condition became methylated post-transfection.
source: Specifically, 23.1% of sites in the unmethylated condition became methylated, while 15.7% of sites in the methylated condition lost methyl marks.
evidence: Supported by bisulfite sequencing analysis

claim: 15.7% of sites in the methylated condition lost methyl marks post-transfection.
source: Specifically, 23.1% of sites in the unmethylated condition became methylated, while 15.7% of sites in the methylated condition lost methyl marks.
evidence: Supported by bisulfite sequencing analysis

claim: The strongest evidence for post-transfection demethylation was observed at K562 ChIP-seq-identified binding sites for ZNF274 (loss of a mean of 35.9% methylation).
source: We observed the strongest evidence for post-transfection demethylation at K562 ChIP-seq-identified binding sites for ZNF274 and GATA2 (loss of a mean of 35.9% and 26.5% methylation, respectively), and for post-transfection de novo methylation at ChIP-seq-identified binding sites for POL2 and KAP1 (gain of a mean 26.0%, and 18.6% methylation, respectively; Supplementary file 9).
evidence: Supported by locus-specific bisulfite sequencing analysis

claim: The strongest evidence for post-transfection demethylation was observed at K562 ChIP-seq-identified binding sites for GATA2 (loss of a mean of 26.5% methylation).
source: We observed the strongest evidence for post-transfection demethylation at K562 ChIP-seq-identified binding sites for ZNF274 and GATA2 (loss of a mean of 35.9% and 26.5% methylation, respectively), and for post-transfection de novo methylation at ChIP-seq-identified binding sites for POL2 and KAP1 (gain of a mean 26.0%, and 18.6% methylation, respectively; Supplementary file 9).
evidence: Supported by locus-specific bisulfite sequencing analysis

claim: The strongest evidence for post-transfection de novo methylation was observed at ChIP-seq-identified binding sites for POL2 (gain of a mean 26.0% methylation).
source: We observed the strongest evidence for post-transfection demethylation at K562 ChIP-seq-identified binding sites for ZNF274 and GATA2 (loss of a mean of 35.9% and 26.5% methylation, respectively), and for post-transfection de novo methylation at ChIP-seq-identified binding sites for POL2 and KAP1 (gain of a mean 26.0%, and 18.6% methylation, respectively; Supplementary file 9).
evidence: Supported by locus-specific bisulfite sequencing analysis

claim: The strongest evidence for post-transfection de novo methylation was observed at ChIP-seq-identified binding sites for KAP1 (gain of a mean 18.6% methylation).
source: We observed the strongest evidence for post-transfection demethylation at K562 ChIP-seq-identified binding sites for ZNF274 and GATA2 (loss of a mean of 35.9% and 26.5% methylation, respectively), and for post-transfection de novo methylation at ChIP-seq-identified binding sites for POL2 and KAP1 (gain of a mean 26.0%, and 18.6% methylation, respectively; Supplementary file 9).
evidence: Supported by locus-specific bisulfite sequencing analysis

claim: GATA family TFs were enriched 6.7-fold among the top 20 TFs ranked by mean loss of methylation (p=3.60×10−4).
source: However, GATA family TFs showed some of the most consistent evidence for demethylation overall: among the top 20 TFs ranked by mean loss of methylation (in the methylated condition), GATA family TFs were enriched 6.7-fold relative to chance expectations (p=3.60×10−4).
evidence: Supported by hypergeometric test of TF family enrichment

claim: The correlation between CpG methylation levels and the expression of the closest gene is relatively strong within a single individual's genome (mean rho = -0.152 ± 0.018 s.d., all p<10−16).
source: In this data set, the correlation between CpG methylation levels and the expression level of the closest gene is relatively strong within a single individual's genome (mean rho = -0.152 ± 0.018 s.d., rho calculated for each of n = 1202 paired genome-wide methylation and gene expression data sets, all p<10−16), but near zero when estimated across individuals (mean rho = 0.008 ± 0.188 s.d., n = 32,843 site-gene pairs measured in 1202 individuals each; Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by analysis of monocyte data shown in Figure 5C

claim: The correlation between CpG methylation levels and the expression of the closest gene is near zero when estimated across individuals (mean rho = 0.008 ± 0.188 s.d.).
source: In this data set, the correlation between CpG methylation levels and the expression level of the closest gene is relatively strong within a single individual's genome (mean rho = -0.152 ± 0.018 s.d., rho calculated for each of n = 1202 paired genome-wide methylation and gene expression data sets, all p<10−16), but near zero when estimated across individuals (mean rho = 0.008 ± 0.188 s.d., n = 32,843 site-gene pairs measured in 1202 individuals each; Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by analysis of monocyte data shown in Figure 5C

claim: In mSTARR-seq identified MD enhancers, there is an enrichment of sites with significant DNA methylation-gene expression correlations across individuals (log2odds = 0.186, p=4.967×10−8).
source: However, in mSTARR-seq identified MD enhancers, there is an enrichment of sites with significant DNA methylation-gene expression correlations across individuals (FDR < 10%), relative to non-MD enhancers (two-sided Fisher's exact test, log2odds = 0.186, p=4.967×10−8).
evidence: Supported by Fisher's exact test comparing MD to non-MD enhancers, shown in Figure 5D

claim: CpG sites found in mSTARR-seq MD regulatory elements are 1.6-fold more common among sites where DNA methylation is strongly negatively correlated with gene expression (rho <−0.2, FDR < 10%).
source: Overall, CpG sites found in mSTARR-seq MD regulatory elements are 1.6-fold more common among sites where DNA methylation is strongly negatively correlated with gene expression (rho <−0.2, FDR < 10%) than among all other sites.
evidence: Supported by enrichment analysis of monocyte data

claim: Increased enhancer activity post-IFNA treatment was significantly correlated with loss of DNA methylation at individual sites (rho = 0.043, p=0.025).
source: Increased enhancer activity post-IFNA treatment was significantly correlated with loss of DNA methylation at individual sites (rho = 0.043, p=0.025; n = 7010 independently analyzed CpG sites), but not significantly correlated with mean loss of CpG methylation across each region (n = 2678, 200 bp regions; rho = 0.014, p=0.687).
evidence: Supported by analysis of IFNA experiment data

claim: The magnitude of the IFNA effect on enhancer activity was a significant predictor of CpG demethylation versus maintenance (p=0.043, R2 = 0.071).
source: The magnitude of the IFNA effect on enhancer activity thus was a significant predictor of CpG demethylation versus maintenance (logistic regression: p=0.043, R2 = 0.071, n = 7010 CpG sites).
evidence: Supported by logistic regression analysis of IFNA experiment data

claim: MD activity is probably less common for CpG sites in the human genome than methylation-independent activity, at least in any given cell type and environmental condition.
source: In particular, our data indicate that MD activity is probably less common for CpG sites in the human genome than methylation-independent activity, at least in any given cell type and environmental condition; further, where it does occur but was missed by our analysis, dependence on DNA methylation is likely to be weak.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that only 15% of enhancers showed MD activity

claim: Both basic sequence characteristics (e.g. density of CpG sites) and the sensitivity of cognate TFs to local methylation play an important role in predicting MD elements.
source: In addition, in agreement with several proposed models for the role of DNA methylation in gene regulation, we find that both basic sequence characteristics (e.g. density of CpG sites) and the sensitivity of their cognate TFs to local methylation play an important role in predicting MD elements (Domcke et al., 2015; Schübeler, 2015).
evidence: Supported by random forests analysis and citations to proposed models

claim: Pioneer TFs, such as members of the GATA TF family, have a higher affinity for methylated DNA.
source: Our results provide support for the hypothesis that pioneer TFs, such as members of the GATA TF family, have a higher affinity for methylated DNA, potentially aiding in their ability to bind condensed chromatin (Zhu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment data and comparison to DNMT knockout data, with citation to Zhu et al., 2016

claim: Methylated fragments that contained endogenous GATA-binding sites tended to become demethylated during the experiments.
source: Indeed, methylated fragments that contained endogenous GATA-binding sites also tended to become demethylated during our experiments, consistent with the role of pioneer TFs in remodeling the epigenome.
evidence: Supported by bisulfite sequencing data showing demethylation at GATA binding sites

claim: MyoD and TCF21 are enriched among MD enhancers with increased activity when methylated.
source: Other TFs important in development and cell fate, such as MyoD and TCF21, are also enriched among MD enhancers with increased activity when methylated, supporting the idea that preferential binding of methylated DNA could be used to aid in pioneer TF discovery (Zhu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis

claim: mSTARR-seq isolates the effects of DNA methylation alone, identifying the subset of MD elements for which changes in DNA methylation are sufficient to causally alter gene regulation.
source: Consequently, mSTARR-seq isolates the effects of DNA methylation alone, identifying the subset of MD elements for which changes in DNA methylation are sufficient to causally alter gene regulation.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the episomal nature of the assay

claim: The effects of DNA methylation on gene expression are cell-type-dependent.
source: Notably, the effects of DNA methylation on gene expression are not only cell-type-dependent, but may also vary depending on environment, genotype, or species (Jirtle and Skinner, 2007; Zhang and Meaney, 2010; Hernando-Herraez et al., 2013; Banovich et al., 2014; Hernando-Herraez et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: The effects of DNA methylation on gene expression may vary depending on environment.
source: Notably, the effects of DNA methylation on gene expression are not only cell-type-dependent, but may also vary depending on environment, genotype, or species (Jirtle and Skinner, 2007; Zhang and Meaney, 2010; Hernando-Herraez et al., 2013; Banovich et al., 2014; Hernando-Herraez et al., 2015).

claim: The pmSTARRseq1 plasmid contains an R6Kγ origin of replication.
source: Problem (i) is unlikely to be an issue for mSTARR-seq because the pmSTARRseq1 plasmid contains the R6Kγ origin of replication, unlike typical plasmids used for high-throughput reporter assays (e.g. STARR-seq (Arnold et al., 2013) and MPRAs (Melnikov et al., 2012)), which are built from the popular pGL3/4 family of plasmids.
evidence: Supported by plasmid design description

claim: A transcription start site was predicted within the pGL3 origin of replication but not within the pmSTARRseq1 origin of replication.
source: Importantly, when we applied a computational algorithm for prediction of eukaryotic PolII promoters (Knudsen, 1999) to pGL3 and pmSTARRseq1, a transcription start site was predicted within the pGL3 origin of replication but not within the pmSTARRseq1 origin of replication.
evidence: Supported by computational promoter prediction analysis

claim: K562s have inactive cGAS/STING pathways.
source: Problem (ii) is also unlikely to affect our mSTARR-seq experiments because K562s have inactive cGAS/STING pathways (the major avenue through which cells sense cytoplasmic DNA and induce an IFN-I response (Muerdter et al., 2018)).
evidence: Supported by citation to Muerdter et al., 2018 and confirmed by qPCR experiments

claim: Plasmid transfection did not induce an IFN-I response in the K562 cell line (p>0.05 for 5/6 genes tested).
source: In agreement with previous work, we found little evidence that plasmid transfection induced an IFN-I response in the K562 cell line (two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test comparing RNA abundance in untransfected versus transfected cells: p>0.05 for all genes tested except OAS3, where p=0.047; Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Power to detect enhancer activity increased with larger query fragment sizes.
source: Notably, power to detect enhancer activity increased with larger query fragment sizes (Figure 2B) and the trade-off between sensitivity and specificity also improved (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), possibly because short fragments eliminate binding sites key to enhancer activity.
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: The current data set is more sensitive to strong enhancers than weak enhancers.
source: Indeed, our results indicate that the current data set is more sensitive to strong enhancers than weak enhancers (Figure 3A), and that we likely miss some true weak and/or weakly MD enhancers, after FDR correction for multiple testing (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 2A and supplementary figures

claim: The functional importance of DNA methylation for gene expression at any given site should be tested empirically and not assumed as a default.
source: Our findings indicate that a minority of CpG sites in the genome have MD regulatory activity. Thus, the functional importance of DNA methylation for gene expression at any given site should be tested empirically and not assumed as a default.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the finding that only 15% of enhancers showed MD activity
